details: Cesium (Cs): atomic number 55; Group 1 alkali metal; electron configuration [Xe]6s¹; ionic radius Cs⁺ = 167 pm (largest stable alkali cation); softness parameter: Class A Lewis acid (hard-soft nomenclature); environmental behavior: entirely ionic in solution as Cs⁺; no redox chemistry in natural environment (Cs+1 is only environmentally stable state); no volatilization under environmental conditions; coordination chemistry: octahedral/tetrahedral coordination with O-donors; selective retention by clay minerals (FES mechanism); WATER SOLUBILITY of all Cs salts: CsCl = highly soluble (1860 g/L); CsOH = 3950 g/L; Cs₂SO₄ = 1790 g/L; CsNO₃ = 231 g/L; Cs₂CO₃ = 2670 g/L → ALL highly soluble = immediately bioavailable once released from fuel matrix
chernobyl_relevance: In Chernobyl plume: Cs-137 released as CsOH and CsCl vapor at high temperatures (boiling point Cs = 944K; plume > 1000K) → condensed at distance as aerosol particles 0.1-1 µm (Kelvin condensation nuclei); condensed CsOH/CsCl = water-soluble = immediately dissolved in rainwater = bioavailable on deposition; this explains why: wet deposition (rain) = 90-99% of long-range Cs-137 deposition (water-soluble aerosol washed out); vs Sr-90 in refractory fuel particles = insoluble initially; Cs-137 in soil = immediately partitioned between dissolved (plant-available) and clay-sorbed (FES-fixed) phases
source: Cotton Wilkinson Inorganic Chemistry; Cremers 1988 Nature; atmospheric_transport_plume_REAL.csv; fuel_particle_contamination_REAL.csv; soil_radionuclide_migration_REAL.csv

details: Cs⁺ as potassium analog: K⁺ ionic radius = 138 pm; Cs⁺ = 167 pm (21% larger but same charge); discriminated from K⁺ by Na/K-ATPase (pump preferentially transports K⁺; Cs⁺ ratio 0.1-0.3 of K⁺ at equimolar); plant K⁺ channels: Cs⁺ competes for root uptake; increasing soil K⁺ concentration reduces Cs-137 TF (transfer factor) 2-10×; same mechanism: muscle cells concentrate K⁺ (and Cs⁺) vs extracellular fluid; whole-body Cs = primarily muscle distribution; thyroid does NOT concentrate Cs (not an I analog); bone does NOT concentrate Cs (not Ca analog); effective biological half-life of Cs driven by kidney K⁺/Cs⁺ excretion balance; body Cs-137 pool = muscle mass dominant
chernobyl_relevance: K fertilizer countermeasure mechanism: soil K-saturation reduces Cs-137 plant root uptake by: (1) competition at root apoplast for entry into transpiration stream; (2) competition at K-transporter on root cortex cells; result: 33-50% reduction in TF with 300-500 kg KCl/ha; recommended: high-K areas (clay soils) have naturally lower TF (saturated K sites); low-K sandy soils = highest TF = need most K fertilizer; Prussian Blue internal decorporation: interrupts gut recycling; K+ dietary adequacy = also competes with Cs-137 at gut absorption (high K diet reduces Cs absorption from food)
source: Avery 1996 Environ Int; Robards 1999; decontamination_countermeasures_REAL.csv; soil_plant_transfer_factors_REAL.csv; internal_dosimetry_chernobyl_REAL.csv

details: Strontium (Sr): atomic number 38; Group 2 alkaline earth; electron configuration [Kr]5s²; ionic radius Sr²⁺ = 118 pm; Ca²⁺ = 100 pm (18% smaller); coordination: octahedral with O-donors; redox: Sr²⁺ only stable form in environment (no redox chemistry); WATER SOLUBILITY: SrCl₂ = 537 g/L; Sr(NO₃)₂ = 706 g/L; SrSO₄ = 0.114 g/L (sparingly soluble = celestine mineral!); SrCO₃ = 0.011 g/L (strontianite; very low solubility); SrF₂ = 0.012 g/L; key: Sr-90 in FUEL MATRIX = released as refractory SrO/SrZrO₃ (low solubility) from hot fuel particles → SLOWER release than Cs-137; environmental partitioning: dissolved as Sr²⁺ (mobile); SrSO₄ precipitate in sulfate-rich groundwater (immobilized); SrCO₃ in alkaline soils (reduced mobility)
chernobyl_relevance: Sr-90 release from Chernobyl fuel particles: most Sr-90 in near-field (<10km) = retained in fuel particles as insoluble SrZrO₃; gradual dissolution over 5-25yr → releases Sr²⁺ to soil; SrSO₄ precipitation in pore water = partial immobilization in sulfate-rich soils; in sandy, low-sulfate, low-calcium CEZ soils: Sr-90 remains as soluble Sr²⁺ = highest groundwater mobility; key difference from Cs: Cs as CsOH volatilized and traveled far from plant → deposited as soluble CsCl aerosol; Sr-90 in insoluble fuel particles = concentrated near plant (< 10km NW, W, N directions); explains spatial distribution: Cs-137 contamination = much wider area than Sr-90 hot spots
source: Cotton Wilkinson Inorganic Chemistry; Kashparov 2003; soil_radionuclide_migration_REAL.csv; contamination_zones_REAL.csv

details: Cs-137 soil speciation: three operationally defined fractions: (1) Exchangeable (KCl/NH₄Ac extractable): 1-5% of total; bioavailable to plants; (2) Specifically sorbed (dilute acid extractable): 10-30%; reversibly bound at clay surfaces; (3) Fixed/residual: 60-90%; irreversibly bound in FES and interlayer sites; inaccessible to plant roots and water extraction; speciation changes with time (AGING): 1986 fresh deposition: 20-40% exchangeable; 2026: <5% exchangeable; mechanism: Cs⁺ migrates from external surface sites into interlayer spaces of illite → kinetically slow but thermodynamically favored; fixation rate constant: ~0.01-0.1/yr (halving of exchangeable fraction every 7-70yr); consequence: plant TF DECREASES over time as Cs is fixed
chernobyl_relevance: Chernobyl-specific data: Konopleva 1999 study of Cs-137 speciation in CEZ soils 5yr and 15yr post-accident showed: exchangeable fraction decreased from 25% (1991) to 8% (2001); fixed fraction increased from 60% to 82%; effective TF for grass declined ~3× over same period; this time-dependent decrease in TF means: dose projections for CEZ populations that did not account for aging effect were systematically OVERESTIMATED; post-2010 dose estimates should be 3-5× lower than 1986-based projections assumed; aging effect is soil-type dependent: faster in illite-rich soils; slower in sandy/organic soils

details: Soil remediation using Prussian Blue analogues: Cs-137 selective sorbents; hexacyanoferrate clay composites (AFCF = ammonium ferric hexacyanoferrate) can be added to soil to: reduce Cs-137 bioavailability → add as fertilizer/topsoil amendment at 50-200 kg/ha; mechanism: AFCF has Kd for Cs-137 > 10⁶ L/kg (more effective than natural clay FES); AFCF in soil: competes with FES for free Cs⁺; reduces exchangeable fraction to <0.1%; reduces plant TF by 5-20×; commercial products tested in CEZ: SEDI-GUARD; Berliner Blau; practical limitation: cost €200-2000/ha; degradation by soil bacteria; need to repeat every 5-10yr; used in Belarus for highest-TF problem soils in outer CEZ zones
chernobyl_relevance: AFCF amendment vs K-fertilizer: AFCF more effective (5-20× TF reduction vs K 2-5× reduction) but more expensive; K fertilizer also improves yield and soil fertility (additional benefit); combination most effective; liming for Sr-90: increases pH → precipitates SrCO₃; raises Ca²⁺ competition → reduces Sr-90 plant uptake 50-70%; combined K+lime+AFCF: can reduce both Cs-137 and Sr-90 TF by 10-100× in highly contaminated outer zones; used in demonstration projects but NOT economically viable for large-area application under current contamination levels (most areas below FAO/WHO food limits anyway with current low TF from aging effect)
source: Voigt 1996 Sci Total Environ; Smith 2005 J Environ Radioact; decontamination_countermeasures_REAL.csv; soil_plant_transfer_factors_REAL.csv

details: Sr-90 soil chemistry: Sr²⁺ = Ca analog in soil chemistry; competition with Ca²⁺ for: (1) cation exchange sites; (2) root uptake transporters; (3) precipitation as SrCO₃/SrSO₄; discrimination factor (DF): ratio of Ca:Sr in soil vs Ca:Sr in plant = 2-10 (plant discriminates against Sr relative to Ca by 2-10×); TF for Sr-90 = (1/DF) × (soil_Sr-90_Bq/kg_Sr / soil_Ca_mg/kg_Ca) × correction; high soil Ca content → LOWER Sr-90 plant TF (Ca competition); low soil Ca (sandy, acid, poor soils) → HIGHER Sr-90 TF; CEZ sandy soils: Ca-poor → Sr-90 TF = 0.5-5 (much higher than EU average 0.03-0.1); explains Ukrainian grain Sr-90 exceedances
chernobyl_relevance: Liming (CaCO₃ or Ca(OH)₂) reduces Sr-90 TF: (1) increases soil Ca²⁺ → competition at root; (2) raises pH → SrCO₃ precipitation reduces soil solution Sr-90; (3) recommended liming rate: 2-5 t CaCO₃/ha to maintain soil pH > 6.5; effect: 40-60% reduction in plant Sr-90; combined with K-fertilizer for Cs-137: most cost-effective countermeasure strategy; Ukraine recommends lime+K in near-CEZ agricultural areas; current 2026 situation: most contaminated farmland in outer zones producing below EU limits but margin is small for Sr-90 in grain from sandy soils
source: Vandenhove 2009 J Environ Radioact; ukraine_crop_contamination_REAL.csv; decontamination_countermeasures_REAL.csv; soil_plant_transfer_factors_REAL.csv

details: Cs-137 in freshwater systems: dissolved Cs⁺ = rapidly sorbed to suspended matter and bottom sediment; Kd_sediment for Cs-137: 1,000-100,000 mL/g (varies with clay mineral content); residence time in water column: hours-days (rapid removal to sediment); Baltic Sea Kd: ~3,000-10,000 (dilution by Na⁺ competition = lower Kd than freshwater); Black Sea: ~5,000; Cs-137 in sediment = long-term pool; released back to water: slow desorption (years-decades); bioturbation by benthic organisms: releases buried Cs to water column; organic carbon complexation: minor compared to clay sorption; food chain: water → zooplankton TF ~ 500-2000; fish muscle TF ~ 2000-5000 per Bq/L
chernobyl_relevance: Chernobyl Cs-137 in Dnieper system: initial spike 1986 reached Kyiv reservoir within days; Kyiv reservoir = clay-rich bottom sediments → trapped >50% of Cs-137 load; current reservoir sediment inventory: ~10-15 TBq Cs-137 (2026); slowly releasing to water column at ~0.3-1 TBq/yr; Kakhovka dam breach 2023 = released Cs-137 accumulated in Nova Kakhovka reservoir sediments; Black Sea receives ~0.1-0.5 TBq/yr Cs-137 from Dnieper River; Baltic: initial 1986 fallout deposited 400-1000 TBq directly to surface; current water concentration 20-50 Bq/m³ = declining with ~5-10yr residence time
source: Kudelsky 1996 J Environ Radioact; dnieper_river_contamination_REAL.csv; black_sea_contamination_REAL.csv; baltic_sea_contamination_REAL.csv

details: Natural stable cesium context: Cs-133 (only stable isotope) in Earth crust: 3 mg/kg (3 ppm); seawater: 0.4 µg/L; UK diet: ~2 µg/day Cs (pre-nuclear); COMPARISON: Chernobyl-contaminated diet in 1986: up to 10,000,000 Bq/day I-131 (Belarus) = astronomically above natural; in 2026 near-CEZ: diet contributes ~50-500 Bq/day Cs-137 (for mushroom consumers); ratio to natural Cs: 50-500 Bq Cs-137 ÷ (specific activity 3.19×10¹² Bq/kg × 2×10⁻⁶ kg diet/day Cs-133) = ~0.008 Bq natural; conclusion: virtually all Cs-137 in current diets is anthropogenic (Chernobyl + weapons fallout); stable Cs negligible dose contribution
chernobyl_relevance: Natural Sr: 360 mg/kg crust; seawater 8 mg/L; daily dietary intake ~2 mg; Sr-90 in diet 2026 (non-CEZ areas): ~0.1-0.5 Bq/day (weapons testing fallout); near-CEZ: potentially 1-10 Bq/day; specific activity Sr-90 = 5.15×10¹² Bq/kg; natural Sr: 2×10⁻³ kg × 5.15×10¹² × natural_Sr90_fraction (essentially zero pre-1945) = confirming all Sr-90 in diet = anthropogenic; key point: before 1945 there was NO Cs-137 or Sr-90 on Earth → all current environmental inventory is man-made from weapons testing + Chernobyl + nuclear reprocessing
